title: Pre-travel consultation: vaccines and travel health
desc: This station involves taking a focused pre-travel history from a young adult planning a long rural trip through mainland Asia, interpreting their immunisation record, and counselling on risk-based vaccines, malaria prevention, food and water safety and return-fever safety-netting.
stem:
You are a general practice registrar in a suburban General Practice clinic. A 31-year-old woman has booked a pre-travel consultation. She is a new patient and is generally well. She plans to travel in 5 weeks. Her immunisation history statement from the Australian Immunisation Register is shown below. You have 2 minutes reading time, then 8 minutes in the station.

VaccineRecorded
Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR)1 dose at 12 months
Diphtheria-tetanus-pertussisLast booster (dTpa) at 15 years, school program
Hepatitis B3 doses, complete, school program
HPVComplete, school program
Hepatitis A, typhoid, Japanese encephalitis, rabies, influenzaNil recorded
tasks: Take a focused travel history from the patient (3 minutes).
Interpret her immunisation record and counsel her on your recommended vaccines, malaria prevention, food and water advice and safety-netting for during and after travel (5 minutes).
patient:
Profile: 31-year-old woman (she/her), not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, office worker, General Practice clinic.

Opening statement: "I'm going travelling in five weeks and want to know what vaccines and tablets I need."

Travel history (give if asked):

  • Backpacking for 6 weeks through Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, flying out in 5 weeks.
  • Mostly rural: village homestays, trekking in forested northern Cambodia and southern Laos, cycling past rice paddies. A few days in cities.
  • Plans to eat street food, may drink tap or ice. Expects contact with stray dogs and monkeys at temples, and has been told she can pat them.
  • No stopover in Africa or South America.

Other history:

  • Well. No medications other than a combined oral contraceptive pill. NKDA. No egg allergy or previous vaccine reaction. No immune problems, no steroids, no splenectomy.
  • Not pregnant, not planning pregnancy for a year, last period 2 weeks ago, pill taken reliably.
  • No previous overseas travel to the tropics. Records match the statement; no other vaccines.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: "I assume I just need a malaria tablet."
  • Concerns: cost and "lots of needles". Worried about getting sick on a trip with no flexibility.
  • Expectation: a clear list of what is essential versus optional.

Cues and questions to ask the candidate:

  • "Do I really need Japanese encephalitis and rabies vaccines? They sound rare."
  • If live vaccines are mentioned: "Can I have them all in one visit?"
  • "What should I do if a monkey scratches me?"
  • "What if I get a fever after I'm home?"
guide:
A high-performing candidate takes a focused travel history, identifies that the trip is long and rural, and recognises the single MMR dose and old dTpa booster as catch-up items. They recommend hepatitis A, typhoid, Japanese encephalitis and discuss rabies with reasons, plan live-vaccine spacing, explain malaria chemoprophylaxis per eTG with bite avoidance, and safety-net clearly for fever within 3 months of return and for animal bites. They address cost and needle concerns and prioritise the plan.

A borderline candidate offers only a malaria tablet and a generic vaccine list, misses the MMR and dTpa gaps, does not ask about pregnancy before live vaccines, and gives vague return advice such as 'see a doctor if unwell' without stating the 3-month window and urgency.
explain:
Approach

A pre-travel consultation is risk-based: itinerary, duration, rural exposure and activities, then host factors (pregnancy, immune status, allergies). The record is checked first for routine catch-up, then travel vaccines are added.

Catch-up

Adults born 1966 or later need 2 documented MMR doses, and measles circulates in parts of Asia. A tetanus-containing booster is advised if more than 10 years since the last dose when travelling to areas with limited access to care.

Travel vaccines

Hepatitis A and typhoid are recommended for most travellers to this region. Japanese encephalitis is recommended for 1 month or more in endemic rural areas. Rabies pre-exposure vaccination is considered for extended rural travel with animal contact. Live vaccines are given the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and are avoided in pregnancy.

Malaria and safety-netting

Chemoprophylaxis agent and timing are chosen per eTG alongside bite avoidance. Any fever during travel or within 3 months of return needs urgent malaria testing. A bite requires wound washing for 15 minutes and urgent post-exposure treatment even if vaccinated.
points: Take a travel history covering destinations, rural or urban, duration, activities, timing before departure, pregnancy, immune status and routine vaccine record.
Adults born 1966 or later need 2 documented MMR doses; check and give catch-up before travel.
Hepatitis A and typhoid vaccines are recommended for travel to much of Asia; give at least 2 weeks before departure where possible.
Japanese encephalitis vaccine is recommended for 1 month or more in endemic rural areas, or shorter stays with high-risk activities.
Give live vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and avoid them in pregnancy.
Malaria prevention combines chemoprophylaxis per eTG with bite avoidance (DEET or picaridin, nets, long clothing at dusk and dawn).
refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook. Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care. Available at: https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au (chapters: Vaccination for international travellers; Japanese encephalitis; Rabies and other lyssaviruses; Typhoid; Hepatitis A; Measles).
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG): Malaria prevention for travellers. Therapeutic Guidelines Limited.
Smartraveller. Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Available at: https://www.smartraveller.gov.au

check.x: Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, explains the purpose of the consultation and uses clear, jargon-free language with appropriate eye contact.

kids.x: Destinations and whether rural or urban [rural Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos with forest trekking and homestays].
Duration and timing before departure [6 weeks, leaving in 5 weeks].
Activities and exposures [street food, tap water, animals, rice paddies, outdoor nights].

check.x: Asks host factors that change vaccine choice: pregnancy or planned pregnancy and contraception, immune status and medications, allergies or previous vaccine reactions, and the routine vaccine record.
Interprets the immunisation record per the Australian Immunisation Handbook:

kids.x: MMR: only 1 recorded dose, so a second dose is needed before travel (2 documented doses for adults born 1966 or later).
dTpa: last booster 16 years ago, more than 10 years, so a booster is advised before travel to a region with limited access to care. Hepatitis B is complete and needs no further dose.

check.x: Recommends vaccines by risk per the Australian Immunisation Handbook:

kids.x: Hepatitis A and typhoid (injectable Vi) recommended; ideally at least 2 weeks before departure.
Japanese encephalitis recommended: 1 month or more with rural exposure in an endemic region. Names the vaccine type and schedule.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination offered for extended rural travel, animal contact and limited access to post-exposure care; explains this does not remove the need for treatment after a bite. Yellow fever not required (no endemic country on the itinerary).

check.x: Plans live vaccines safely: MMR and live-attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart; confirms not pregnant and advises avoiding pregnancy for 28 days after live vaccines.

Malaria: explains risk in the forested areas, advises chemoprophylaxis choice and duration per eTG (start before, during and after leaving the risk area), plus bite avoidance: DEET or picaridin repellent, long clothing at dusk and dawn, permethrin-treated nets.
Gives food and water advice (bottled or boiled water, no ice, well-cooked food, hand hygiene, oral rehydration for diarrhoea) and advises registering on Smartraveller and arranging travel insurance.

kids.x: Any fever during travel or within 3 months of return needs same-day medical review for malaria testing; tells the doctor about the travel.
Animal bite or scratch: wash wound with soap and water for 15 minutes and seek urgent post-exposure treatment, even if vaccinated (vaccinated people still need further doses).

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations (cost, number of needles), prioritises essential versus optional vaccines, checks understanding and books a follow-up visit before departure.
